title: Summers in Atlanta: the 91 Theater and Mr. Bailey
summary: Working summers at his aunt's laundry, he played cornet at the rowdy, dusty 91 Theater owned by Mr. Bailey, who was strict but a fine man.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Where I came from: parents, siblings and birth

blocks.x: No, before that. I would go to Atlanta, during the school's -- summertime, I'd go to Atlanta because I had an aunt there that was married to a Chinaman, and he had a laundry there so I used to go down in the summer and work in the laundry. And I played cornet at the 91 Theater, with Eddie Heywood Hayward's father.
Uh-huh, Eddie Heywood Hayward, Sr.
Ed Heywood Hayward, Sr.
Now the 91 was also owned by Mr. Bailey?
Yes. That was Mr. Bailey's.
Now that was a -- the better theater was the 81?
81 was the better theater, yes.
Yeah.
Oh, yes.
What was the -- really the difference, was it in --
Well the 91 seems as though it was just a makeshift theater --
Uh-huh.

-- it wasn't really built as a theater and the stage was makeshift and the show up there -- the show the dust would fly all over the stage when the dancers would dance and the place would just be full of dust. There was a lot of (unintelligible) and the element that catered to that theater was a low class of people there because they had the worst comedians and the worst blues singers in the world, at that -- what they thought.
Uh-huh.
And it was what you call a rowdy type of a theater.
Do you remember any of them?
No I don't. I'll remember the dancers some of them, they -- I remember cause whenever they'd dance the dust would fly up all over the theater, they'd throw
their feet down on the floor, the planks of the stage -- the place would be just full of dust, I don't -- because it was very comical and that's what the people liked then.
Uh-huh. What about Mr. Bailey, himself, what was he like?
Well he was -- seemed to be a very fineman. And very strict, stern. He kept everything going pretty his way.
Uh-huh.
But he was a very fine man, I thought, you know, for a theater man --
